claim: Early auditory cortex of nonhuman primates represents associations between sounds and actions in both spiking activity and local field potentials.
source: Here, using a go/no-go paradigm and a symmetrical reward, we show that early auditory cortex of nonhuman primates represents such associations, in both the spiking activity and the local field potentials.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sound-evoked neuronal responses in early auditory cortex changed with sensorimotor associations shortly after sound onset.
source: Sound-evoked neuronal responses changed with sensorimotor associations shortly after sound onset, and the neuronal responses were largest when the sound signaled that a no-go response was required in a trial to obtain a reward.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding, supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Neuronal responses in early auditory cortex were largest when the sound signaled that a no-go response was required in a trial to obtain a reward.
source: Sound-evoked neuronal responses changed with sensorimotor associations shortly after sound onset, and the neuronal responses were largest when the sound signaled that a no-go response was required in a trial to obtain a reward.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Association processes take place in the auditory system and do not necessarily rely on association cortex.
source: Our findings suggest that association processes take place in the auditory system and do not necessarily rely on association cortex.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings in the abstract.

claim: Auditory cortex may contribute to rapid selection of appropriate motor responses to sounds during goal-directed behavior.
source: Thus, auditory cortex may contribute to a rapid selection of the appropriate motor responses to sounds during goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons in frontal and prefrontal cortices respond differently to a given stimulus when it signals different actions.
source: Previous studies have shown that neurons in frontal and prefrontal cortices respond differently to a given stimulus when it signals different actions (Asaad et al., 1998; Komatsu, 1982; Sakagami and Tsutsui, 1999; Sakagami et al., 2001; Watanabe, 1986; Yamatani et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Very little is known whether similar representations of associations between stimuli and actions are present in sensory cortices.
source: However, very little is known whether similar representations of associations between stimuli and actions (sensorimotor associations) are present also in sensory cortices.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Representations of sensorimotor associations in sensory cortex might accelerate the selection of appropriate actions via direct anatomical projections from sensory cortex to motor cortex.
source: If so, this might accelerate the selection of the appropriate action because such representations might be directly conveyed to motor cortex via anatomical projections from sensory cortex to motor cortex (Matyas et al., 2010; Scheich et al., 2007), and not only indirectly via cortical association areas.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction, supported by citations about anatomical projections.

claim: Auditory cortex is known to be more than a mere stimulus processor.
source: To our knowledge, only few studies have investigated whether learned sensorimotor associations are represented in sensory cortex and specifically in auditory cortex, which is known to be more than a mere stimulus processor (Scheich et al., 2011; Weinberger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several studies reported that neurons in early auditory cortex responded differently to a given sound depending on the action the animal had to execute in response to the sound.
source: Several studies reported that neurons in early auditory cortex responded differently to a given sound depending on the action the animal had to execute in response to the sound (David et al., 2012; Jaramillo et al., 2014; Vaadia et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Observed differences in neuronal responses to sounds in auditory cortex do not necessarily reflect differences in sensorimotor associations but perhaps differences in confounding factors.
source: However, the observed differences in the neuronal responses do not necessarily reflect differences in sensorimotor associations but perhaps differences in confounding factors known to affect neuronal activity in auditory cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a critical evaluation of previous studies in the introduction.

claim: Confounding factors that affect neuronal activity in auditory cortex include the events used to cue the animal about the association between sound and action.
source: These factors include the events used to cue the animal about the association between sound and action (Brosch et al., 2005; Brosch et al., 2015; Rodgers and DeWeese, 2014; Vaadia et al., 1982), the acoustic context in which the sound was embedded (Brosch and Scheich, 2008; Brosch and Schreiner, 1997; Brosch et al., 1998; Brosch et al., 1999; Jaramillo et al., 2014; Nelken and Ulanovsky, 2007; Ulanovsky et al., 2003), and the valence of the sound, that is the associated type of reinforcement (Blake et al., 2006; David et al., 2012; Rutkowski and Weinberger, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Two macaque monkeys were each trained to perform two tasks requiring different sensorimotor associations.
source: Two macaque monkeys were each trained to perform two tasks requiring different sensorimotor associations.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design in the Results section.

claim: In both tasks, a trial started with the illumination of a light emitting diode (LED) where upon the monkeys had to grasp and hold a touch bar for several seconds.
source: In both tasks, a trial started with the illumination of a light emitting diode (LED) where upon the monkeys had to grasp and hold a touch bar for several seconds (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The monkeys received the reward for correct go responses (hits) and correct no-go responses (correct rejections) and no reward for incorrect responses (misses and false alarms).
source: The monkeys received the reward for correct go responses (hits) and correct no-go responses (correct rejections) and no reward for incorrect responses (misses and false alarms).
evidence: This describes the reward structure of the experimental paradigm.

claim: In Task 1, the go response was required for the sequence 3–3 and the no-go response for the other sequences.
source: In Task 1, the go response was required for the sequence 3–3 and the no-go response for the other sequences.
evidence: This describes the task structure as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Task 2, the go response was required for the sequence 1–1 and the no-go response for the other sequences.
source: In Task 2, the go response was required for the sequence 1–1 and the no-go response for the other sequences.
evidence: This describes the task structure as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The monkeys were cued which task to perform in a trial, with a green LED located to the monkey's right for Task 1 and with a red LED located to the monkey's left for Task 2.
source: The monkeys were cued which task to perform in a trial, with a green LED located to the monkey's right for Task 1 and with a red LED located to the monkey's left for Task 2.
evidence: This describes the cueing method used in the experimental design.

claim: Nearly all d-prime values were >1 across all experimental sessions for both monkeys in both tasks.
source: Note that nearly all d-prime value were >1.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and shown in the figure.

claim: For the example multiunit, the spike rate during the presentation of an S1 of 3 kHz was higher in Task 2 than in Task 1.
source: For this example, the spike rate during the presentation of an S1 of 3 kHz (orange traces) was higher in Task 2 (Figure 2Bi) than in Task 1 (Figure 2Ai), that is the spike rate was higher to S1-no-go than to S1-uncertain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: For the example multiunit and for the 3 kHz tone, the during-S1 spike ratio was 1.40, which was significantly >1.
source: For this multiunit and for the 3 kHz tone, the during-S1 spike ratio was 1.40, which was significantly >1 (p<0.05, permutation test).
evidence: This is stated as a specific result from the example multiunit.

claim: During-S1 spike ratios for all 298 multiunits for the 3 kHz tone ranged from 0.38 to 2.78, with a median of 1.09 which was significantly >1.
source: These ratios ranged from 0.38 to 2.78, with a median of 1.09 which was significantly >1 (p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated as a summary statistic for all multiunits, shown in Figure 2Ci.

claim: Ratios significantly different from 1 were obtained for 124 of the 298 multiunits (41.6%) for the 3 kHz tone, with the majority of these ratios being >1 (81.5%).
source: Ratios significantly different from 1 (that is >1 or <1; green dots) were obtained for 124 of the 298 multiunits (41.6%; 95 of the 226 multiunits [42.0%] for monkey C and 29 of the 72 multiunits [40.3%] for monkey L), with the majority of these ratios being >1 (81.5%).
evidence: This is stated as a summary statistic for all multiunits, shown in Figure 2Ci.

claim: Significant during-S1 spike ratios occurred more frequently in the 35 multiunits with a best frequency within a range of ±0.5 octaves around 3 kHz than in the other 263 multiunits (57.1% vs. 39.5%).
source: Significant during-S1 spike ratios occurred more frequently in the 35 multiunits with a best frequency within a range of ±0.5 octaves around 3 kHz than in the other 263 multiunits (57.1% vs. 39.5%; p<0.05, chi-square test).
evidence: This is stated as a result relating best frequency to the occurrence of significant ratios.

claim: The median of the before-S1 spike ratio distribution was 0.97, which was not significantly different from 1.
source: However, the median of the distribution was 0.97, which was not significantly different from 1 (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis of before-S1 spike ratios.

claim: Significant before-S1 spike ratios were observed less frequently than significant during-S1 spike ratios (88 of 298, 29.5% versus 124 of 298, 41.6%).
source: Also, significant before-S1 spike ratios (black dots) were observed less frequently than significant during-S1 spike ratios (88 of 298, 29.5% versus 124 of 298, 41.6%; p<0.05, chi-square test, one-tailed), and significant before-S1 spike ratios >1 were not overrepresented (33 of 88, 37.5%).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between before-S1 and during-S1 spike ratios.

claim: For the multiunits having significant during-S1 spike ratios, the during-S1 spike ratios were generally larger than the corresponding before-S1 spike ratios.
source: For the multiunits having significant during-S1 spike ratios, the during-S1 spike ratios were generally larger than the corresponding before-S1 spike ratios (Figure 2Cii), and for only a minority of these multiunits were the before-S1 spike ratios also significant (47 of 124, 37.9%; filled dots) while for the majority they were not (77 of 124, 62.1%; open dots).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2Cii.

claim: Significant during-S1 spike ratios occurred less frequently in the passive condition than during task performance (19.2% vs. 41.6%).
source: Significant during-S1 spike ratios occurred less frequently in the passive condition than during task performance (19.2% vs. 41.6%; p<0.05, chi-square test, one-tailed).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between passive and task conditions.

claim: At least 18.5% of the multiunits (55/298) in early auditory cortex represent sensorimotor associations of S1.
source: Overall, therefore, at least 18.5% of the multiunits (55/298) in early auditory cortex represent sensorimotor associations of S1.
evidence: This is stated as a conservative estimate after accounting for confounds.

claim: The average normalized spike rates to S1-no-go and S1-uncertain started to differ ~70 ms after tone onset, persisted throughout the tone, and disappeared shortly after tone offset.
source: The average normalized spike rates to S1-no-go and S1-uncertain started to differ ~70 ms after tone onset, persisted throughout the tone, and disappeared shortly after tone offset (Figure 2E, compare orange and purple traces).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For the example multiunit, the spike rate to S2-no-go in Task 2 was higher than to S2-go in Task 1 for the 3 kHz tone.
source: For example, for the 3 kHz tone, the multiunit in Figure 2A and 2B exhibited a higher spike rate to S2-no-go in Task 2 (Figure 2Biv, orange trace) than to S2-go in Task 1 (Figure 2Aii, orange trace).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: During-S2 spike ratios for the 3 kHz tone ranged from 0.38 to 3.11, with a median of 1.13 which was significantly >1.
source: During-S2 spike ratios for the 3 kHz tone (Figure 2Di, green curve) ranged from 0.38 to 3.11, with a median of 1.13 which was significantly >1 (p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2Di.

claim: Significant during-S2 spike ratios were obtained for 108 of 294 multiunits (36.7%), with the majority of these significant ratios being >1 (80.6% of 108).
source: Significant during-S2 spike ratios (green dots) were obtained for 108 of 294 multiunits (36.7%). The majority of these significant ratios were >1 (80.6% of 108).
evidence: This is stated as a summary statistic for all multiunits, shown in Figure 2Di.

claim: The median of before-S2 spike ratios was 0.98 which was not significantly different from 1.
source: Before-S2 spike ratios (Figure 2Di, black curve) ranged from 0.39 to 2.59, with a median of 0.98 which was not significantly different from 1 (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis of before-S2 spike ratios.

claim: Significant before-S2 spike ratios were observed less frequently than significant during-S2 spike ratios (21.4% vs. 36.7%).
source: Significant before-S2 spike ratios (black dots) were observed less frequently than significant during-S2 spike ratios (21.4% vs. 36.7%; p<0.05, chi-square test, one-tailed; compare black and green dots in Figure 2Di), and significant before-S2 spike ratios >1 were not overrepresented (42.9%; 27 of the 63 significant ratios).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between before-S2 and during-S2 spike ratios.

claim: Significant during-S2 spike ratios occurred less frequently in the passive condition than during task performance (13.1% vs. 36.7%).
source: For the 3 kHz tone, significant during-S2 spike ratios occurred less frequently in the passive condition than during task performance (13.1% vs. 36.7%; p<0.05, chi-square test, one-tailed).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between passive and task conditions.

claim: At least ~20% of the multiunits recorded in auditory cortex (64/294) represented sensorimotor associations of S2.
source: Therefore, ~20% of the multiunits recorded in auditory cortex (64/294) represented sensorimotor associations of S2.
evidence: This is stated as a conservative estimate after accounting for confounds.

claim: The normalized spike rates to S2-go and S2-no-go started to differ shortly after tone onset, persisted throughout the tone, and disappeared shortly after tone offset.
source: Similar to S1, the normalized spike rates to S2-go and S2-no-go, geometrically averaged across multiunits with significant during-S2 spike ratios, started to differ shortly after tone onset, persisted throughout the tone, and disappeared shortly after tone offset (Figure 2F, compare purple and orange traces).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Spike rates in auditory cortex increased and peaked shortly (~200 ms) before the bar release.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 4A shows the average normalized spike rates with reference to the time of bar release executed after S2-go, revealing that spike rates in auditory cortex increased and peaked shortly (~200 ms) before the bar release.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Multiunits generally responded more strongly to S2-no-go than to S2-nil, with a median spike ratio of 1.10 which was significantly >1.
source: Analyses similar to those described above revealed that multiunits generally responded more strongly to S2-no-go than to S2-nil, with a median spike ratio of 1.10 which was significantly >1 (p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test; orange curve in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A; for an example multiunit, compare the orange traces in Figure 2Biv and Figure 2Aiv).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: There was no difference in the spike responses to S2-go and S2-nil: the median spike ratio was 1.00, not significantly different from 1.
source: However, there was no differences in the spike responses to S2-go and S2-nil: the median spike ratio was 1.00, not significantly different from 1 (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test; purple curve in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A; for an example multiunit, compare the orange traces in Figure 2Aii and Figure 2Bii).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The normalized spike responses to S2-no-go were significantly stronger than those to S1-uncertain, S2-go and the two S2-nils.
source: The normalized spike responses to S2-no-go were significantly stronger than those to S1-uncertain, S2-go and the two S2-nils and the normalized spike responses to S1-no-go were significantly stronger than those to S1-uncertain, S2-go, and the two S2-nils (p<0.05/4, each corrected for multiple pairwise comparisons, Wilcoxon signed rank test; compare orange and purple curves; for detailed p values, see Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The spike response to a given tone in auditory cortex was strongest when the tone, irrespective of whether it was presented as S1 or as S2, signaled that the no-go response was required in a trial to obtain a reward.
source: These findings show that the spike response to a given tone in auditory cortex was strongest when the tone, irrespective of whether it was presented as S1 or as S2, signaled that the no-go response was required in a trial to obtain a reward.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The spike response to a given tone can change rapidly, on a time scale of one second, depending on the required motor response signaled by the tone.
source: In addition, our finding that the spike responses to S1 and S2 in the same trial differed during task performance (i.e., S1-no-go vs. S2-nil; Figure 3A) but not in the passive condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) indicates that the spike response to a given tone can change rapidly, on a time scale of one second, depending on the required motor response signaled by the tone.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the comparison between task and passive conditions.

claim: The normalized spike responses to S1-no-go in false-alarm trials were smaller than the responses to S1-no-go in correct trials, with a median response ratio of 0.92 which was significantly <1.
source: The responses to S1-no-go in false-alarm trials were smaller than the responses to S1-no-go in correct trials, reflected in the fact that the median of the corresponding response ratios was 0.92, which was significantly <1 (p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The responses to S2-no-go in false-alarm trials were smaller than the responses to S2-no-go in correct trials, with a median of 0.71.
source: Similar results were obtained for the 51 comparisons for S2 such that the responses to S2-no-go in false-alarm trials were smaller than the responses to S2-no-go in correct trials (Figure 4C; black curve; median of 0.71; p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The responses to S2-no-go in false-alarm trials were not significantly different from the responses to S2-go in correct trials, with a median of 0.95.
source: In contrast, the responses to S2-no-go in false-alarm trials were not significantly different from the responses to S2-go in correct trials (gray curve; median of 0.95; p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis of false-alarm trials.

claim: Spike responses to tones that signaled the no-go response in a trial were related to the monkeys' behavior.
source: These analyses show that spike responses to tones that signaled the no-go response in a trial were related to the monkeys' behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis of false-alarm trials.

claim: Sensorimotor associations are represented in the activity of neuronal populations in early auditory cortex as measured by local field potentials.
source: Analysis of the local field potentials (LFPs), which were recorded simultaneously with the spiking activity, revealed that sensorimotor associations are represented also in the activity of neuronal populations in early auditory cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the LFP analysis.

claim: For the example site, both during-S1 and during-S2 LFP ratios were significantly >1.
source: For this site, both during-S1 and during-S2 LFP ratios were significantly >1 (p<0.05, permutation test).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the example site shown in Figure 5.

claim: Significant during-S1 LFP ratios were obtained at 264 of 401 studied sites for the 3 kHz tone, with the vast majority of these ratios being >1.
source: For the 3 kHz tone, we obtained significant during-S1 LFP ratios at 264 of 401 studied sites (green dots in Figure 5Ci) and significant during-S2 LFP ratios at 145 sites (green dots in Figure 5Di), with the vast majorities of these ratios being >1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5Ci.

claim: About 70% of the significant during-S1 LFP ratios (45.0% of all 401 sites) were considered to be due to differences in the sensorimotor associations.
source: Thus, about 70% of the significant during-S1 LFP ratios (45.0% of all 401 sites) and 70% of the significant during-S2 LFP ratios (23.6% of all 401 sites) were considered to be due to differences in the sensorimotor associations.
evidence: This is stated as a conservative estimate after accounting for confounds.

claim: The LFPs represented sensorimotor associations in a way similar to the spike rates.
source: We found that the LFPs represented sensorimotor associations in a way similar to the spike rates: (1) the average normalized LFPs for S1-no-go and S1-uncertain and for S2-no-go and S2-go started to differ shortly after the beginning of the early part of the response and continued throughout the late part of the response (Figure 5E and 5F); (2) the normalized LFP to a given tone was strongest when the tone, irrespective of whether it was presented as S1 or as S2, signaled that the no-go response was required in a trial (Figure 3B; p<0.05/4, each corrected for multiple pairwise comparisons, Wilcoxon signed rank test; for detailed p values, see Figure 3—source data 2); (3) the normalized LFP to a given tone could change rapidly within a trial on a time scale of about one second depending on its sensorimotor associations, with the LFP being stronger when it was S1-no-go than when it was S2-nil (p<0.05/4; Figure 3B); (4) the normalized LFP to the tone that signaled the no-go response depended on the monkeys' behavior (Figure 4B and 4D).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the LFP findings, with references to multiple figures.

claim: The experimental design enabled testing whether sensorimotor associations are represented in auditory cortex by comparing neuronal responses to tones of the same frequency and in corresponding positions in the two tasks.
source: This experimental design should enable testing whether sensorimotor associations are represented in auditory cortex by comparing neuronal responses to tones of the same frequency and in corresponding positions in the two tasks (compare Figure 1C and 1D).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental rationale.

claim: Visual stimuli, eye position, and the mental state related to them might result in phasic or tonic changes of neuronal activity in auditory cortex.
source: Because visual stimuli, eye position, and the mental state related to them might result in phasic or tonic changes of neuronal activity in auditory cortex (Bizley and King, 2008; Brosch et al., 2005; Brosch et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2004; Rodgers and DeWeese, 2014; Werner-Reiss et al., 2003), we assessed potential contributions of the visual cue to differences in the neuronal responses between the tasks by analyzing the neuronal activity during periods directly before S1 and before S2.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Within each experimental session, the monkeys conducted the two tasks in separate, alternating blocks of trials.
source: Within each experimental session, the monkeys conducted the two tasks in separate, alternating blocks of trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A block consisted of ~140 trials and lasted ~25 min.
source: A block consisted of ~140 trials and lasted ~25 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In each block, trials requiring the go response or the no-go response were presented in pseudorandom order, with the go response required in ~60% of the trials and the no-go response in ~40% of the trials.
source: In each block, trials requiring the go response or the no-go response were presented in pseudorandom order, with the go response required in ~60% of the trials (range 50–77%) and the no-go response in ~40% of the trials (range 23–50%).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The median probability for a tone to have a frequency of 3 kHz in Task 1 was about three times that in Task 2.
source: Consequently, the median probability for a tone to have a frequency of 3 kHz in Task 1 was about three times (range 2–6) that in Task 2, and the probability for a tone to have a frequency of 1 kHz in Task 1 was about one third that in Task 2.
evidence: This describes a consequence of the experimental design.

claim: Differences in the probabilities of the 3 kHz and the 1 kHz tones within tasks and across tasks contributed to differences in the acoustic context and could result in different degrees of stimulus-specific adaptation of the neuronal responses.
source: These differences in the probabilities of the 3 kHz and the 1 kHz tones within tasks and across tasks contributed to differences in the acoustic context and could result in different degrees of stimulus-specific adaptation of the neuronal responses (Nelken and Ulanovsky, 2007; Ulanovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a potential confound, supported by citations.

claim: Microelectrode recordings of neuronal activity in auditory cortex started once the monkeys had responded correctly to each of the four sequences in ≥65% of the trials in both tasks during ten consecutive sessions.
source: Microelectrode recordings of neuronal activity in auditory cortex started once the monkeys had responded correctly to each of the four sequences in ≥65% of the trials in both tasks during ten consecutive sessions.
evidence: This describes the criterion for starting recordings.

claim: Single-unit and multiunit spiking activity as well as LFPs were recorded from the core fields of the right auditory cortex of both monkeys.
source: Single-unit and multiunit spiking activity as well as LFPs were recorded from the core fields of the right auditory cortex of both monkeys.
evidence: This describes the recording methods.

claim: This report is based on the data recorded during 243 experimental sessions.
source: This report is based on the data recorded during 243 experimental sessions.
evidence: This describes the dataset.

claim: During 154 of these sessions, the monkeys performed the two tasks.
source: During 154 of these sessions, the monkeys performed the two tasks (108 and 46 sessions from monkey C and L, respectively).
evidence: This describes the dataset.

claim: During nearly all the 154 task sessions, the monkeys discriminated between the go and each of three no-go sequences in both tasks.
source: During nearly all the 154 task sessions, the monkeys discriminated between the go and each of three no-go sequences in both tasks.
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance.

claim: Previous studies that investigated whether auditory cortex represents sensorimotor associations did not control for or estimate potential contributions of various confounds such as the cue, the acoustic context or the valence of sounds.
source: Previous studies that investigated this issue did not control for or estimate potential contributions of various confounds such as the cue (Vaadia et al., 1982), the acoustic context (Jaramillo et al., 2014) or the valence of sounds (David et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a critique of previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The valence confound was not present in the current study due to the symmetrical reward.
source: The latter confound was not present in our study due to the symmetrical reward, that is the monkeys received the same reward for correct go responses and correct no-go responses.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental design.

claim: The neuronal responses in auditory cortex did not reflect what the monkeys should have done, but rather reflected what the monkeys actually did.
source: Therefore, the neuronal responses in auditory cortex did not reflect what the monkeys should have done, but rather reflected what the monkeys actually did.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the false-alarm trial analysis.

claim: Neuronal activity in auditory cortex can be related to an animal's behavior.
source: Our study thus provides further support that neuronal activity in auditory cortex can be related to an animal's behavior (e.g., Bizley et al., 2013; Niwa et al., 2012; Selezneva et al., 2006; Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes of sensorimotor associations were paralleled by changes of the tone-evoked neuronal responses shortly after the beginning of the responses.
source: For both S1 and S2, changes of sensorimotor associations were paralleled by changes of the tone-evoked neuronal responses shortly after the beginning of the responses (Figure 2E and 2F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding, with reference to figures.

claim: The auditory system contributes to the association of a tone with a motor response.
source: This suggests that the auditory system contributes to the association of a tone with a motor response.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the timing of neuronal response changes.

claim: Task-specific changes of the neuronal activity in auditory cortex may result in an enhanced contrast of the neuronal responses to the tones having different meanings in the two tasks.
source: The task-specific changes of the neuronal activity in auditory cortex may result in an enhanced contrast of the neuronal responses to the tones having different meanings in the two tasks, for example by increasing the neuronal responses to a no-go tone.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: Task- and meaning-specific changes may arise from changes of stimulus-specific adaptation, forward suppression, or receptive field properties of neurons in auditory cortex or in earlier stages of the auditory system.
source: Such changes may arise from task- and meaning-specific changes of stimulus-specific adaptation, forward suppression, or receptive field properties of neurons in auditory cortex or in earlier stages of the auditory system (Atiani et al., 2009; Groh et al., 2001; Gruters et al., 2018; Metzger et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: These changes may be mediated by sub-cortical neuromodulator systems, for example cholinergic and dopaminergic nuclei.
source: These changes may be mediated by sub-cortical neuromodulator systems, for example cholinergic and dopaminergic nuclei (Ayala and Malmierca, 2015; Huang et al., 2016b), or by higher-order associative systems, for example prefrontal cortex (Gao et al., 2017; Winkowski et al., 2013; Winkowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Early auditory cortex may contribute to the selection of appropriate motor responses to auditory stimuli.
source: The results of our study suggest that early auditory cortex may contribute to the selection of appropriate motor responses to auditory stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Early auditory cortex appears to be involved in a function that traditionally has been associated with parietal, frontal, and prefrontal cortices.
source: Therefore, early auditory cortex appears to be involved in a function that traditionally has been associated with parietal, frontal, and prefrontal cortices (Asaad et al., 1998; Freedman and Ibos, 2018; Komatsu, 1982; Sakagami and Tsutsui, 1999; Sakagami et al., 2001; Watanabe, 1986; Yamatani et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The results point to a possible communication between auditory cortex and association cortices.
source: Our results thus point to a possible communication between auditory cortex and association cortices (Sheikhattar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The observation that responses were enhanced when tones signaled the no-go response might point to a role of auditory cortex in inhibitory control.
source: This observation might point to a role of auditory cortex in inhibitory control, a process that permits individuals to inhibit their natural or dominant motor response in order to select a response that is consistent with completing their current goals (Chambers et al., 2009; Diamond, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The findings extend the knowledge about the neuronal basis of inhibitory control, which has been obtained mainly by conducting studies in frontal and prefrontal regions.

evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by citations.

claim: Auditory cortex has non-auditory functions including representing non-auditory stimuli, motor behavior, and motivational aspects of tasks.
source: In conclusion, our findings add to other non-auditory functions of auditory cortex, such as representing non-auditory stimuli, motor behavior, and motivational aspects of tasks (Bizley and King, 2008; Brosch et al., 2005; Brosch et al., 2015; Eliades and Wang, 2008; Niwa et al., 2012) and temporarily storing task-relevant information (Huang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by citations.

claim: These functions may be crucial for auditory cortex to integrate diverse task-relevant information to adapt to task demands and thus to serve as a semantic processer or a problem solver.
source: These functions may be crucial for auditory cortex to integrate diverse task-relevant information to adapt to task demands and thus to serve as a semantic processer (Scheich et al., 2011) or a problem solver (Weinberger, 2011), ultimately contributing to the selection and preparation of appropriate motor responses to achieve a given goal in different situations.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by citations.
